Thermal Drift in Low-Cost Widget Strain Sensors | 2026.06.27
Thermal Drift in Low-Cost Widget Strain Sen -
sors
R. Okafor, Materials Lab, L. Petrova, Materials Lab
Corresponding Author: r.okafor@example.org
Abstract
Low-cost resistive strain sensors are attractive for high-volume widget moni -
toring but their accuracy under temperature swings is poorly characterized.
We measured drift across a 10 to 60 degree Celsius range for a batch of forty
sensors and fit a linear compensation model. The model reduced mean absolute
error substantially, suggesting inexpensive sensors are viable when paired with
a software correction.
Keywords: strain sensing, thermal drift, calibration
1 1. Introduction
Resistive strain sensors are widely de -
ployed for structural monitoring, yet
thermal sensitivity limits their use in
uncontrolled environments. Prior work
characterized drift for laboratory-grade
devices but not for the low-cost units
common in high-volume deployments.
2 2. Materials and Meth -
ods
Forty sensors were mounted on a refer -
ence beam and cycled across 10 to 60
degrees Celsius in a controlled chamber.
Resistance was logged at one Hertz and
paired with a calibrated thermocouple
reading.
3 3. Results
Uncompensated readings drifted with
temperature in an approximately linear
fashion across the tested range. A per-
sensor linear correction reduced the
mean absolute error by a large margin.
4 4. Discussion
The linearity of the observed drift makes
a lightweight software correction prac -
tical on constrained hardware. Limita -
tions include the single beam geometry
and the bounded temperature range.
5 5. Conclusion
Low-cost strain sensors are viable for
widget monitoring when paired with a
1

per-sensor linear thermal correction de -
rived from a short calibration sweep.
